title: Coin Change II
statement: You have unlimited coins of several values and a target amount. Count how many different combinations of coins add up to the amount. Two combinations are the same if they use the same coins, whatever order you list them in.

example.caption: Amount 5 with coins 1, 2 and 5 has 4 combinations: 5, 2+2+1, 2+1+1+1 and 1+1+1+1+1.

output.label: dp[i][a] = combinations for amount a using the first i coin kinds

idea.sentence: dp[i][a] counts the combinations for amount a using the first i coin kinds. It is the count without coin i, plus the count with at least one coin i: dp[i-1][a] + dp[i][a-coin].

jargon.plain: A bag of coins where order does not matter. 1+2 and 2+1 are the same combination.
A sequence where order matters. 1+2 and 2+1 are two different permutations.

watch.inputHint: Two arguments: the amount, then the coin list, e.g. 5, [1,2,5]

compare.unit: steps (rough; combinations can grow exponentially, drawn as 2n)

rows.name: Brute force
rows.note: Recurse on (coin index, amount left). Many calls repeat.

rows.name: 2-D table
rows.note: One cell per (coins allowed, amount). Easy to see, and to trace.

rows.name: One rolling row
rows.note: Row i reads row i-1 (the same cell) and itself (a - coin). So one array works: for each coin, for a from coin up, dp[a] += dp[a - coin].

fast.takeaway: Put the coins in the outer loop. Each combination is then built in one fixed coin order, so it is counted once. Put the amounts outside and you count orders instead.

stages.title: Base row and column
stages.note: Row 0 means no coins, so only amount 0 works (1 way). Column 0 is 1 in every row.

stages.title: Without this coin
stages.note: Copy the cell above: the ways that never use coin i. It is the only choice when the coin is bigger than the amount.

stages.title: With this coin
stages.note: Add the cell a - coin steps to the left in the same row: take one coin i, then make the rest with the same coins.

stages.title: Read the corner
stages.note: The bottom-right cell allows every coin and the full amount.

edges.title: Amount 0
edges.why: There is exactly one way to make nothing: take no coins. That is why column 0 is 1, not 0.

edges.title: Order must not count
edges.why: 1+1+1 and 1+2 are the only combinations. 2+1 is the same bag as 1+2. Amount in the outer loop would say 3.

edges.title: No way
edges.why: Only even amounts can be made. The cell for amount 3 stays 0.

edges.title: A coin larger than the amount
edges.why: Coin 5 can never be used, so its row just copies the row above. The a >= coin check stops a negative index.

gotchas.text: Loop order is the whole trap. Coins outside, amounts inside counts combinations. Amounts outside, coins inside counts permutations (1+2 and 2+1 both). The Demo shows the two side by side.
Check a >= coin before reading dp[i][a - coin]. Otherwise the index goes negative.
A negative array index returns undefined, not an error, and undefined + number is NaN. A missing a >= coin check will quietly poison the table.
A negative index panics. The counts can pass 2^31 for large inputs, so keep them in int (64-bit on most machines) or use int64.

recap.pattern: 2-D DP: take or skip the coin
recap.key: dp[i][a] = dp[i-1][a] + dp[i][a - coin_i]. Coins in the outer loop, so combinations are counted once.
recap.complexity: Time O(k·A). Space O(k·A), or O(A) with one row.
moves: Table of (k+1) rows by (amount+1) columns; column 0 is 1
For each coin (outer loop), for each amount a
dp[i][a] = dp[i-1][a], plus dp[i][a-coin] if a >= coin
